extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students working on classical analytic geometry and conic-section constructions
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations, constructions, and theorems about hyperbola and parabola sectors/polygons and the theory/procedures of polar reciprocal curves and surfaces (including formulae and geometric constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transformations to produce integrable differential equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply successive variable transformations (choose new dependent/independent variables and introduce parameters) so as to obtain forms in which certain terms vanish (e.g. choose parameters to make T = 0 or S = 0) and thereby reduce the equation to one that can be integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each transformation increases chances of integration and yields relations between coefficients that define integrable cases; alternative transformations may simplify obtaining new coefficients directly without elimination. Follow the examples: set T = V + ... to force T = 0, or set 7r = 0D + ... to make S = 0, then operate accordingly to integrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between e and powers of unity when passing to series
rubrics_metrics.description: When transitioning from an exponential function to its series (or when manipulating expressions like e^{i·something} with non-integer indices), do not conflate multipliers or assume powers of unity behave as ordinary integer powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid neglecting multiplicative factors when equating series expressions; the paradoxes (e.g. concluding e = 1) arise from failing to track multipliers or the distinction between e and ±1^α when indices are not whole numbers. Carefully track factors and the domain of indices when comparing series and their equivalent functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction A — divide a hyperbolic sector into n equal areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Given hyperbolic sector PiOPn with asymptotes OC and OD, construct points P1..Pn dividing the sector into n equal sectors by drawing parallels to asymptotes through interpolated points on an asymptote segment; computed proportions follow equations (8),(9),(10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from base endpoints draw parallels to one asymptote to meet the other; partition the segment on the asymptote in n−1 proportional parts (found algebraically via equations (8)-(10)), then draw parallels to the other asymptote through those partition points to meet the curve. The proportional points generally must be computed numerically except in special geometric cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction B — maximum n‑gon inscribed in hyperbolic segment
rubrics_metrics.description: The maximum polygon of n sides inscribed in a hyperbolic segment has the property that the tangent at each vertex is parallel to the opposite chord; the vertex positions satisfy the same proportional relations as in (A) (equations (13),(14) coincide with (8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To construct: find points P1...Pn as in (A) (division of base by computed proportions) and join them in order to obtain the maximum inscribed n‑gon. Use tangent–chord parallelism to verify maximality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction C — minimum (n+1)‑gon circumscribed about hyperbolic segment
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimum polygon of n+1 sides circumscribed about a hyperbolic segment is formed by tangents at the same set of points P1...Pn; the minimality condition leads to relations (e.g. equation (19)) which coincide with the equal‑sector relations (8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: find P1...Pn as in (A), draw tangents at these points and take their intersections to form the circumscribed polygon. Minimality can be shown by the derived algebraic condition (19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property D (hyperbola) — angular points lie on concentric similar hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: The angular (contact) points of a minimum polygon circumscribed about a hyperbolic segment lie on a concentric hyperbola similar to the given hyperbola; the two hyperbolas are concentric and similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from algebraic relations among coordinates of tangency points (see equations (17),(21),(23)). Use to deduce locus of contact points when constructing minimal circumscribed polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property E (hyperbola) — duality between circumscribed and inscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: If PiRiRj... is the minimum polygon of n+1 sides circumscribed about the segment PiPn and RiRn−1 is joined, then the polygon Ri...R_{n−1} is the maximum polygon of n−1 sides inscribed in the segment RiR_{n−1} of the hyperbola in which the points Ri... lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geometric duality: joining appropriate intersection points of tangents yields the maximal inscribed polygon in the corresponding subsegment; construction (C) and (B) are dual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property F (hyperbola) — sides of maximum inscribed polygon touch a concentric similar hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: The sides of a maximum polygon inscribed in a hyperbolic segment are tangents that touch a concentric similar hyperbola (i.e., there exists a concentric similar hyperbola tangent to all sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the converse viewpoint of (D): given a maximum inscribed polygon, its sides are tangent to some concentric similar hyperbola; useful when building inscribed polygons from tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction b — maximum n‑gon inscribed in parabolic segment
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabolic segment PiPn, divide the base chord into n−1 equal parts Q1...Q_{n−1}; through these points draw lines parallel to a diameter (i.e., parallel to the axis direction) meeting the arc to produce P1...Pn, giving the maximum inscribed n‑gon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place conjugate axes so that the axis of x coincides with the diameter that bisects the chord; the equal partition of the chord (equation (23) / (24)) gives the required contact points. This construction is purely geometric and simpler than hyperbolic case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction c — minimum (n+1)‑gon circumscribed about parabolic segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Tangents at the points found in (b) intersect to form the minimum polygon of n+1 sides circumscribed about the parabolic segment PiPn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in the hyperbolic case, find P1...Pn via equal divisions of the base and draw tangents at those points; their intersections yield the minimal circumscribed polygon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property d (parabola) — angular points lie on equal parabola with same axis
rubrics_metrics.description: The angular/contact points of a minimum polygon circumscribed about a parabolic segment lie on a parabola equal to the given one, and the two parabolas have their principal axes in the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parallels hyperbola property (D): the locus of contact points is an equal parabola whose axis coincides with that of the given parabola. Use (24),(29),(30) for coordinate relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property e (parabola) — duality between circumscribed and inscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: If PiRi... is the minimum circumscribed polygon of n+1 sides about parabolic segment PiPn and R_i R_{n−1} is joined, then the polygon R_i... is the maximum polygon of n−1 sides inscribed in the corresponding subsegment where those Ri lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the parabolic analogue of (E) for hyperbola; join intersections of tangents to get the inscribed polygon in the derived subsegment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property f (parabola) — sides of maximum inscribed polygon touch equal parabola
rubrics_metrics.description: The sides of a maximum polygon inscribed in a parabolic segment are tangents to an equal parabola whose principal axis coincides with that of the given parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This complements (d): given a maximum inscribed polygon, its sides are tangent to a parabola equal to the original, aiding dual constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I — polar of a point with respect to a conic; equation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line through P meets a given conic in Q and Q' and P and P' are conjugate harmonic points with respect to Q and Q', then the locus of P' (the polar of P) is a straight line whose equation is given by (2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic derivation: substitute parametric values and use quadratic root relations to get the polar's equation (2). Use this to compute the polar line of any point relative to a conic via coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem II — reciprocity of polars
rubrics_metrics.description: If the polar of a point P passes through another point R, then reciprocally the polar of R passes through P; the pole of a line is the intersection of polars of any two points on that line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equation (3) condition to test incidence; this reciprocity is fundamental for polar constructions and for finding poles of given lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem III — reciprocal curves as envelopes/loci of poles
rubrics_metrics.description: Two curves are polar reciprocals (with respect to a director) when the points of one are poles of tangents applied to the other; reciprocally the points of the second are poles of tangents to the first (each curve is the envelope of the polars of points of the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limiting processes (letting points approach tangency) to show tangents/poles correspondence; this relation underlies all constructions of reciprocal curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem IV — tangent/diameter parallelism in reciprocal curves
rubrics_metrics.description: A tangent applied to one of the reciprocal curves at any point is parallel to the ordinates of the diameter of the director that passes through the corresponding point of the reciprocal curve. For director = circle, the radius to a point is perpendicular to the tangent at the corresponding point on the reciprocal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, compute equations of ordinates and tangents (see formulae in IV) to verify parallelism and perpendicularity for circle directors; use this to relate local directions between reciprocal curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure V — compute polar reciprocal of a conic with respect to a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a conic (4) and the unit circle as director, the reciprocal curve's equation is obtained by equating the tangent of the given conic at (x',y') with the polar x x' + y y' = 1 and eliminating fractions to produce equation (5). Coordinates of the reciprocal point are the reciprocals of tangent intercepts on axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the tangent formula, write polar condition x x' + y y' = 1, eliminate x',y' to obtain explicit equation (5). Use derived formulae to identify type (parabola/hyperbola) and asymptotes by coefficient conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of reciprocals (consequences of V) — type and geometric correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed consequences include: (1) If B^2 − AC = 0 then the reciprocal passes through the director's centre (parabola ↔ passes through centre); (2) If D^ = AF = 0 then one curve touches an axis and the reciprocal is hyperbola with asymptote parallel to the other axis; (3) When certain coefficients vanish, axes of reciprocals are parallel; (4) when D ≠ 0 and F = 0 axes correspond to tangent/normal, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coefficient conditions in derived reciprocal equation (5) to infer geometric character and mutual relations (e.g. where asymptotes and tangents are perpendicular to particular lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure VI — compute polar reciprocal with respect to a general conic director
rubrics_metrics.description: Given director (8) and curve (9), form tangent at a point and the polar of the reciprocal point; equate and eliminate to get the reciprocal curve's equation (e.g. equations (12),(14)), enabling many derived theorems about diameters, centers and types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow algebraic elimination steps in the text to produce explicit reciprocal equations; then apply coefficient comparisons to deduce special cases (parabolic reciprocals, diameters, centers' polars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem — similar conics and harmonic pencils of their reciprocal intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: When two conic sections are similar, their polar reciprocals intersect in two straight lines passing through the pole of the line joining their centres, and those conjugate common secants together with polars of the centres form a harmonic pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarity relations of coefficients between the two conics and the algebraic elimination given in (7) to deduce the two straight lines; apply to families of similar conics sharing a centre line to find common secants of reciprocals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem — polar reciprocals of concentric conics intersect on director centre lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If two conic sections are concentric, their polar reciprocals with respect to a director intersect on two straight lines passing through the director's centre; the director's centre is an intersection point of conjugate common secants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set centres equal in the algebraic formulae (leading to reduced relations) to obtain the two straight lines; useful to identify secants and symmetry in reciprocal curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem — reciprocals with respect to a parabola and shared focus property
rubrics_metrics.description: If a system of conic sections has the principal vertex of a parabola for a common focus, then the polar reciprocals of any two of them (taken with respect to that parabola) have a common secant which touches the parabola at that vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the special elimination under parabola-as-director (see derived relations) to locate the common secant tangent to the director at its vertex; applies to focal system symmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus problem (XIII) — pole of chord joining radii with fixed angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two radii from a fixed point making a given angle, the locus of the pole of the chord joining their extremities is given by an explicit algebraic relation derived by eliminating parameters (see final formula in the section), relating coefficients of the conic and the fixed angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form the three equations (conic, chord line, radius line), eliminate to get a polynomial whose roots give directions; then compute the pole of the chord via the polar equation. Use the provided elimination steps and final expression.
